sections.h2: What batch and expiry tracking is for
paras: If what you sell has a shelf life, a quantity on hand is not enough information to despatch against. You need to know which batch each unit belongs to, when that batch expires, which batch should go out next, and later, which customer received which batch. Aura Business does this through the Batch and Expiry Tracking module in the Inventory and Warehouse suite.

Two things follow from having batches. Picking can be first-expiry-first-out, so the stock closest to its date leaves first instead of whatever is nearest the door. And traceability works in both directions: from a batch to every customer who received it, and from a customer complaint back to the batch and the supplier it came from.

sections.h2: Expired stock is money you already paid for, sitting on a shelf.
sections.lead: It is also the one inventory loss that is entirely predictable, and that is what makes it so annoying when it happens.

items.p: The cartons at the front of the rack are the ones that arrived last, so the older batch quietly ages out.
A date is noticed while packing an urgent order, and now the order cannot go and nothing was reordered.
Reagents arrive with weeks left on them, the lab refuses them, and the return costs you twice.

items.h: No idea who got which batch
items.p: The supplier reports a problem with one lot and you cannot say which customers received it.
The expiry loss surfaces once a year in a single unpleasant number.

items.h: Batch numbers not on the invoice
items.p: Customers who need batch details for their own records keep ringing your office for them.

sections.h2: From goods receipt to the customer who received it.

steps.p: The GRN records batch number, expiry date and quantity for each lot from the supplier.
The batch holds its own quantity in whichever godown or branch it went into.
Stock approaching expiry is flagged while it is still worth selling or returning.
Despatch proposes the batch nearest its date, so old stock moves before new.
Batch number and expiry appear on the delivery challan and tax invoice lines.
Any batch can be listed with the customers it went to, and any customer line traced back to its batch.
Expired stock is removed as a reasoned adjustment rather than an unexplained quantity change.

items.q: Can an item have several live batches at once?
items.a: Yes. Each batch holds its own quantity, expiry date and location, so the same product can sit in three batches across two godowns and the system still knows which one should be despatched next.

items.q: Does it force us to despatch the earliest-expiry batch?
items.a: It is the proposed pick, not a lock. Some customers require a minimum remaining shelf life on arrival, so the picker can choose a different batch and the choice is recorded against the despatch.

items.q: How early do the alerts fire?
items.a: Near-expiry thresholds are set to suit what you sell, because a reagent with a short life needs warning much earlier in relative terms than a disposable with a two-year date.

items.q: Does the batch number print on the invoice?
items.a: Yes. Batch and expiry carry through from the picked stock onto the delivery challan and the GST tax invoice lines, so customers who need them for their own records get them without ringing you.

items.q: Can we trace a batch to its customers?
items.a: Yes. Any batch can be listed with every despatch that carried it, and any invoice line can be traced back to the batch and the goods receipt it came from. See warehouse management.

items.q: Does this apply to serialised equipment too?
items.a: Serialised machines are tracked by serial number rather than batch, and both models run side by side. Consumables carry batches, capital equipment carries serials. See inventory software.
